title: A Great Decision Without Vigorous Execution Might as Well Be a Lousy Decision
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The post argues that leaders over-invest in making decisions and under-invest in the buy-in needed to carry them out. A decision resisted by the people who must implement it is, in practice, a poor one. The author recommends gaining subscription early: involve implementers while the decision is forming, explain the why, and share the underlying data so people feel ownership. Drafting an execution plan before the decision is finalized can also improve the decision itself. The conclusion is that flawless execution matters more to organizational outcomes than the quality of the decision on paper.
points: Execution quality, not decision quality alone, determines whether a decision stays great.
Involving implementers early and giving them a voice builds ownership that survives setbacks.
Clarifying the why and sharing the data before a decision is final earns buy-in.
Building an execution plan during the decision process can reveal consequences and refine the choice.
quotes: Too many leaders miss an essential insight about quality decision-making: A great decision is entirely dependent on quality execution to remain great.

Leaders overly focused on decision-making and not enough on the subscription and buy-in it takes to institute the decision are often surprised that their hard work in crafting the decision is all for naught.
They involve those who will be tasked with execution early on, giving them a voice while the decision is being shaped.
When team members understand the need for the decision and get to explore some or all the data used to make the choice, they feel a sense of ownership for the decision.
Leaders are commonly taught that making quality decisions is what matters most. In reality, it is execution that makes the biggest difference in organizational outcomes.
